Hi Jamie,

Thanks for the clear list — helpful. Short answers up front and then a proposed action plan: 

1) Notifications: Yes — Redwood can emit an automated "backup lifecycle" notification when a snapshot transitions to DELETED state (post-retention). By default we send a single email to the account admins and an event into the customers configured webhook endpoint within 24 hours of the state change. The notification contains: snapshot id, regions affected, timestamp, and a retention-policy id.

2) Legal hold after prune: If a snapshot was pruned from a secondary region but still present in the primary region or in immutable offsite storage, we can mount a restore within the standard emergency restore window. For hosted customers the default emergency restore window is 30 days after the DELETED state; for Dedicated customers we can extend to 90 days via contractual SLAs. If the snapshot is already fully expired in all tiered stores, recovery requires our cross-region recovery process and may not be possible beyond the configured retention periods.

3) Hosted vs Dedicated differences: Hosted is subject to global retention tiers and cross-region replication schedule (typically 24-72h replication). Dedicated gives an option to pin retention/replication and to enable a retention override policy that pauses deletion while a manual legal hold is being evaluated.

Below are the concrete runbook steps we follow when a legal hold request arrives referencing backups: 

- Step 0: Intake — customer opens an evidence/legal hold request via support portal or the account webhook; we create an incident record.
- Step 1: Hold evaluation (2 business hours) — CS triages whether the snapshot id(s) are still present in any tier (primary, replicated, offsite archive).
- Step 2: Retention override (if available) — for Dedicated or Enterprise customers we can apply a retention-override token which transitions the snapshot into an "immovable" state for up to 90 days while legal performs discovery. This prevents scheduled GC.
- Step 3: Emergency restore (if snapshot still exists) — Infra can perform a prioritized restore; estimated ETA depends on total data size (typical for Acme profiles: 4-12 hours).
- Step 4: Post-restore: we provide integrity hashes and audit logs (KMS key id, rotate history) to meet evidence needs.

If the snapshot has already been purged from every tier (including immutable archive), we will still provide the audit timeline and cross-region deletion evidence but the binary contents are unrecoverable.

FYI: technical clarifications on deletion propagation and KMS impacts.

On Tue, Jun 15, 2027 at 10:05 AM Marissa Cole wrote:
> Below are the concrete runbook steps we follow when a legal hold request arrives referencing backups: 

Details: 
- Deletion propagation timeline: when a snapshot enters DELETED in region A, the replication controller marks the shadow copy in region B for GC. The earliest GC sweep runs 48 hours post-state-change; subsequent sweeps occur daily for 14 days. Most snapshots are purged from secondaries inside 3-14 days depending on region replication backlog.
- Immutable/offsite archives: we keep daily immutable archives for 90 days in the standard plan; these archives are subject to encryption key availability.
- KMS considerations: if a KMS key used to encrypt a snapshot is scheduled for rotation or scheduled deletion, it can affect our ability to decrypt archived copies. We recommend customers avoid scheduling KMS key deletion while pursuing a legal hold.
- Emergency snapshot resurrection: If a snapshot is still decryptable and present in an offsite archive, we can resurrect it to a recovery cluster; typical prep time for Acme-size dataset is 6-18 hours.

If Acme needs tighter guarantees (for example, guaranteed 90-day hold for any prune event), we should model this as a retention-override add-on in the SOW so its enforced at the orchestration layer and not reliant on manual intervention.
